lines: Break one AI agent, and you learn one thing: it broke.
Look closer. This model walks into the same wall eleven times, sure it is one step from the goal.
This one wanders into a dead end, and resets far too late.
Now break thousands of them, on games none of them has ever seen.
The pieces stop being noise. They line up.
Every failure points at something agents still can't do. We built a factory that finds those things.
The agent sees only this: sixty-four by sixty-four pixels, sixteen colours. No text, no score, no rule names.
It has six buttons. That's all.
Colours and shapes are reshuffled for every game, so nothing can be memorised.
Each new level hides one new rule, and the agent has to discover it by experimenting.
And every level is proven solvable by search, so we always know the best possible run.
We ran frontier models on games nobody had seen. First with our own harness.
Then the way labs benchmark them: the full conversation, and maximum reasoning effort.
None of them matches the optimal reference run.
Every failure is a decision we can point to.
This model is sure that moving right reaches the goal. The screen never changes.
This one resets far too late.
This one acts on a belief the screen has already disproved.
Everything they needed was on the screen.
The score rewards solving levels efficiently, and nothing else.
On the judges' own harness, doing nothing scores zero. Stopping after one level earns only that level.
Resetting never erases the moves already spent.
And the score is computed in a separate container that the agent cannot reach.
Then we asked: can a small model learn from this experience?
We compare it against a control trained on the same amount of non-game data, so any gain comes from the games, not just from more training.
A factory of fresh, verified games is useful beyond this hackathon: private evaluations that can't leak, and training environments for labs.
Every broken agent shows where AI still has to learn.
Try to beat the AI yourself.
